name: The Stress Test
description: A 90-minute, 4-round advanced Express simulation on supervisory stress testing and bank capital planning, for courses in bank management, financial institutions, risk management and corporate finance. Merrow Valley Bancorp (a fictional Category IV regional bank in Columbus, Ohio, with 118 billion dollars of assets): as CFO you run the 2028 capital-planning cycle against the stress capital buffer the Federal Reserve sets with its own models. You decide the stress scenario and how office loan losses are projected, the dividend and the buybacks in the capital plan, the answer to the Fed number and the gap between your models and the supervisor, and the distributions and balance sheet when office loans default. Scored on the headroom over the requirement, the capital returned net of market reactions, the accuracy of your own projection, supervisory findings and net income.
view:
The Stress Test

A year as CFO of a US regional bank: build the stress test, size the dividends and buybacks against a buffer the Federal Reserve sets with its own models, answer the Fed’s number and hold the line when the office loans default.

Merrow Valley Bancorp · Columbus, Ohio · Office of the CFO You are the team of Maya Lindqvist, CFO since January 2028 of a bank with $118 billion of assets, $9.45 billion of CET1 capital and a CET1 ratio of 10.27%. 2028 is a supervisory stress-test year: the Fed will set the stress capital buffer (SCB) with its own models, and the requirement will be the 4.5% minimum plus that buffer. In the 2026 cycle the bank projected the 2.5% floor and the Fed set 3.4%. The CEO has promised investors a 20% dividend increase and $1.6 billion of buybacks. Every round is measured on the decisions taken so far.

Round 1 · Monday 14 February 2028: the scenarios are out

The Fed has published the 2028 scenarios: in the severely adverse one unemployment rises to about 10% and commercial real estate prices fall by about 40%. The capital plan, with your projections, is due on Wednesday 5 April. Merrow Valley holds $7.5 billion of office loans, much of it refinancing in 2028 and 2029. Run as they are, your loss models — estimated on 2010–2019 data — project 7% office losses over nine quarters; Priya Raman, from model risk management, warns that the model has never seen an office downturn. You decide the plan’s scenario: the Fed’s severely adverse scenario only, as in the last cycle; the Fed’s plus Merrow Valley’s own scenario built on its office book and its uninsured deposits ($2 million of internal work); a milder in-house downturn as the planning scenario; or a consultant’s generic severe scenario (Harlow & Pierce Advisory, $1.2 million). And how the office losses are projected: the models as they are; a documented overlay from a loan-by-loan review, independently validated ($1.5 million); a $300 million management overlay agreed in the CFO’s office; or a 25% cut because “our borrowers are better than the market”.

The Fed does not use your models: it sets the buffer with its own. Your projection is only useful if it resembles the Fed’s for good reasons.

Round 2 · Monday 27 March: the capital plan goes to the board

The plan sets the dividend from the third quarter and the buybacks from July 2028 to June 2029. Today the dividend is $0.30 a share a quarter ($600 million a year, 500 million shares); the first half of 2028 is already committed ($300 million of dividends and $400 million of buybacks). The dividend is inside the buffer: four quarters of planned dividends, divided by $92 billion of risk-weighted assets, are added to the scenario’s CET1 decline. Buybacks are not, but they draw on the same capital. Thomas Harrigan, the CEO, wants in the plan what he promised in November. You decide the quarterly dividend: $0.27 (a 10% cut, $540 million a year); $0.30 (hold, $600 million); $0.33 (+10%, $660 million); or $0.36 (+20%, $720 million, as promised). And the buybacks from July 2028 to June 2029: none; $400 million; $800 million (the last program’s pace); or $1.6 billion (as promised).

A bank sizes its distributions against the Fed’s number plus a buffer of its own, not against its own number.

Round 3 · Monday 26 June: the Fed’s number

The Fed has published the results. Merrow Valley’s buffer is 3.77% with the dividend held (3.71% with the cut, 3.84% with +10%, 3.90% with +20%): with the dividend held, the requirement from 1 October is 8.27%. You have two business days to adjust planned distributions and fifteen days to ask for the buffer to be reconsidered. You decide the answer: keep the distributions as submitted; resize the buybacks to keep a 1.5-point management buffer over the requirement at every quarter-end of the plan (the cut is announced); request reconsideration and pause buybacks until the answer; or keep the buybacks and issue $500 million of noncumulative perpetual preferred stock at 7.25% to add capital. And what to do about the gap between your models and the Fed’s: nothing, the Fed’s models are conservative by design; set an overlay each year so your losses match the Fed’s; a challenger model and the Fed’s published loss rates, with overlays reviewed quarterly by model risk management ($1.5 million); or redevelop the office model with independent validation ($12 million, nine months).

Not all capital counts the same: the requirement is measured in Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1).

Round 4 · Monday 13 November: the office loans default

Two large office borrowers have defaulted. The office book will charge off 6% in the fourth quarter ($450 million) and a further 3% ($225 million) is expected in the first half of 2029. Banks whose models under-projected office losses must also rebuild their allowance. Below the requirement, distributions are limited to a maximum payout amount (Regulation Q). You decide the distributions for the fourth quarter and the first half of 2029: continue the buybacks and the dividend; pause buybacks and keep the dividend; halve the dividend and stop buybacks; or accelerate: $500 million of extra buybacks in the fourth quarter while the stock is down. And the balance sheet: keep growing loans to budget ($1.0 billion more risk-weighted assets by year-end and $2.0 billion more by June 2029); freeze loan growth; a synthetic risk transfer on $6 billion of prime auto and mortgage loans ($3.6 billion less risk-weighted assets; $15 million of cost in the fourth quarter and $18 million in the first half of 2029); or sell $2 billion of office loans at 85 cents on the dollar ($300 million loss).

In a downturn, capital is protected first by the balance sheet and the buyback; the dividend is the last thing to touch.
